analysis.one_liner: Guarantees every American comprehensive health coverage through regulated private plans or state single-payer systems.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Labor Committee on the day it was introduced, never gained a single cosponsor, and died without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have guaranteed every U.S. citizen and legal resident a comprehensive health insurance package — hospital care, prescription drugs, mental health services, and free preventive care — through regulated private plans, with states allowed to run single-payer systems instead. Insurers could no longer deny anyone coverage or charge sick people more, low-income families would get premium discounts, and employers would have to contribute and offer at least three plan choices. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured Americans gain a guaranteed, comprehensive benefit package that insurers could not deny based on health status, with community-rated premiums so sick people pay the same as healthy ones. Low-income families gain premium discounts and cost-sharing reductions, everyone gains free preventive and prenatal care and a ban on balance billing, and patients gain a consumer advocate office in every state to help resolve disputes. People with disabilities gain new home and community-based care, and people 35 and over could buy into a new public nursing-home insurance program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured Americans and people with pre-existing conditions

how_it_helps.text: Creates a universal entitlement: every eligible individual is entitled to comprehensive benefits including hospital care, physician services, outpatient prescription drugs, mental health and substance abuse treatment, and clinical preventive services with no cost-sharing, and plans are barred from balance billing patients [S2][S3].
Bars insurers from denying, limiting, or conditioning coverage for any reason including health status, and requires guaranteed renewal so no one can be dropped for getting sick [S3].

Requires community rating: within a rating area the standard premium is the same for every plan and every person, adjusted only for family class and capped age factors, ending the practice of charging sick or older people far more [S3].
Gives low-income families — AFDC and SSI recipients and families below income thresholds — premium discounts, cost-sharing reductions, and limits on repayment liability [S2].

Requires every employer to offer each employee a choice of at least three certified plans and to withhold and forward premium contributions, with a cap on how much of a low-wage worker's pay the premium can consume [S2].
Lets states adopt a single-payer system operated by the state as an alternative to the regulated private-plan market [S3].

Establishes consumer advocacy offices in every state and a national center to help people enroll, apply for subsidies, and resolve grievances with plans and providers, with conflict-of-interest rules keeping the offices independent of insurers and providers [S3].

Adds new public benefits: home and community-based services for people with disabilities, a voluntary public nursing-home insurance program for adults 35 and over, payments to hospitals serving low-income patients, and grants for community health centers, school health services, and mental health programs [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers bear the largest cost: they lose the ability to deny coverage, must accept everyone at community rates, face premium limits and financial solvency requirements, and are barred from forming or controlling purchasing cooperatives. Employers must pay a required share of premiums for their workers. The bill's suggested financing — a higher cigarette tax, a phased-in premium assessment, and a payroll assessment on exempt employers — is stated only as the committee's sense of what should accompany the Act, not enacted in the bill itself. Patients injured by malpractice would see limits on attorney fees and on recovering full damages. Tobacco companies and private long-term care insurers lose revenue.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, employers, and tobacco companies

drawbacks.text: Every eligible individual is required to enroll in a plan and pay any required premium, so families who find even subsidized premiums or the family share unaffordable would face a legal obligation to buy coverage [S3].

The bill contains no enacted financing: the cigarette tax increase, premium assessment, and payroll assessments appear only as a statement that Congress 'should include' these funding sources, leaving the entire cost of the new entitlement, subsidies, and federal payments unfunded in the bill's actual text [S2][S3].

The malpractice title limits attorneys' contingency fees, reduces damages where collateral sources cover the loss, and forces parties into state-run alternative dispute resolution before suing — lowering the compensation available to patients genuinely injured by medical negligence [S2].

Small employers (10 or fewer employees with wages under a set amount) are exempted from employer premium-payment obligations, so workers at the smallest businesses would carry more of their own premium cost [S2].

The bill exempts providers and facilities from delivering any covered service that violates their religious belief or moral conviction, with no express remedy stated for a patient denied care on that ground [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — guaranteed comprehensive coverage that no one can be denied, priced the same for sick and healthy alike — is large and would have directly addressed the era's tens of millions of uninsured. The honest counterweights are real: the individual mandate could burden families if subsidies fell short, the bill deliberately leaves all financing to future legislation, small-business workers are carved out of employer contributions, and malpractice limits would cut compensation for injured patients in exchange for lowering providers' liability costs. The design keeps private insurers as the delivery channel rather than replacing them, which is why it was a moderate rather than single-payer approach — though states could have opted into single-payer.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on January 5, 1995, the first day of the new 104th Congress, and delivered introductory remarks [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day [S5].
The action record shows no further steps — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — through the end of the 104th Congress on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers, large employers, and private long-term care insurers were better off because the bill died: they avoided guaranteed-issue and community-rating requirements, mandatory premium contributions, and a public nursing-home insurance competitor. Americans who were uninsured or paying high rates for pre-existing conditions remained without guaranteed coverage.

for.name: Sen. Edward M. Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 104th Congress and delivered introductory remarks; he was the bill's only sponsor and it drew no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — during the two-year life of the Congress

against.name: Senate Republican majority
against.role: Newly controlling party in the 104th Senate
against.what_they_did: Controlled the chamber's agenda after the 1994 elections and did not schedule or pursue comprehensive universal-coverage legislation

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the only recorded sign of support was one Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors, and the Senate had just flipped to Republican control after the 1994 elections.

industries.note: The bill keeps private insurance as the delivery channel — certified plans, purchasing cooperatives, and employer plans all remain — but strips its most profitable practices: guaranteed issue, community rating, bans on health-status discrimination and balance billing, premium limits, and a prohibition on insurers forming or controlling purchasing cooperatives. Insurers would have kept a permanent regulated role while losing underwriting profit from cherry-picking healthy customers.

Large employers must offer experience-rated certified plans, contribute a set share of premiums, and face federal corrective action if their health spending grows too fast — shifting the burden of coverage onto them and away from workers.
The bill creates a voluntary public nursing-home insurance program for adults 35 and over and bars insurers from selling duplicative long-term care policies, eliminating a private market segment.
A specified increase in the cigarette tax is named as a funding source for the Act, though only as the committee's recommendation rather than enacted text.

Federal malpractice limits — mandatory alternative dispute resolution, caps on contingency fees, and reduced damages for collateral-source recovery — lower liability exposure for providers and their insurers, at the cost of reduced compensation for injured patients.

The bill mandates federal payments for graduate medical education, medical school operating costs, and the indirect costs academic health centers bear for teaching and research, funded from premium revenues.

industries.industry: Community health centers and safety-net hospitals
industries.note: New grants for community health groups, rural hospitals, school-based health sites, and the National Health Service Corps, plus entitlement-style payments to hospitals serving high shares of low-income and Medicare/Medicaid patients.
